# Sherlock Scenario
As a fast-growing startup, Forela has been utilising a business management platform. Unfortunately, our documentation is scarce, and our administrators aren't the most security aware. As our new security provider we'd like you to have a look at some PCAP and log data we have exported to confirm if we have (or have not) been compromised.

## Artifacts provided.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

## Skills Learnt

- Network packet capture analysis with Wireshark and tshark
- Zeek alert analysis
- Parsing json data with jq
- Use of the "Wayback Machine" in Incident Response
- An understanding of different types of brute force attacks
- Alignment of the attack chain to MITRE ATT&CK

## Zeek alerts

Zeek is a passive, open-source network traffic analyzer tool. It analyzes network traffic packets and creates “Zeek logs” which can be used to detect malicious activity within a network.
Different types of network metadata, like Zeek logs, IPFIX and NetFlow, allow better visibility into specific network conversations (or flows).

**The json file here is a series of Zeek alerts that have been output in json format.**

The [Zeek documentation](https://docs.zeek.org/en/master/log-formats.html) describes ways to parse this using the 'jq' tool. This tool allows many ways to manipulate, search and filter the content to find what we're looking for.
To begin we will install jq using

``sudo apt install jq``


We can now start to investigate the alerts using the following command to firstly remove the outer json list and secondly pipes the command into less allows us to navigate through the output

``jq '.[]' meerkat-alerts.json | less``

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
## Packet Capture

The ``pcap`` file is a network packet capture.  There are many ways to capture such a file including the incredibly popular [Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/).
To open the ``pcap`` in Wireshark on ParrotOS or other similar operating systems use ``wireshark meerkat.pcap``

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**


# Questions

## We believe our Business Management Platform server has been compromised. Please can you confirm the name of the application running?

**There are two ways we can proceed:**
We can extract the zeek logs in Json format using 
``jq '.[]' meerkat-alerts.json | less`` and look for any alert that seems suspicious. 

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
or we can  filter by ``alert.signanture`` using  ``jq '.[].alert.signature' meerkat-alerts.json`` This will list all packet signatures, allowing us to quickly identify any suspicious information.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

## We believe the attacker may have used a subset of the brute forcing attack category - what is the name of the attack carried out?

The vulnerability seen in question 1 is explained [here](https://rhinosecuritylabs.com/application-security/cve-2022-25237-bonitasoft-authorization-bypass/)
The exploit relies on a finding a legitimate username and password combo to allow privilege escalation and ultimately code execution as long as that user has a valid session token at the time of the exploit. This does indicate that an attacker would potentially look to use a Brute Forcing technique on the application to find some valid credentials, but doesn't tell us enough about what type of brute force attack was taking place.

Looking at the [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/) page on the Brute Force technique we see it has the

following sub-techniques:

- **Password Guessing:** Adversaries with no prior knowledge of legitimate credentials within the system or environment may guess passwords to attempt access to accounts.

- **Password Cracking:** Adversaries may use password cracking to attempt to recover usable credentials, such as plaintext passwords, when credential material such as password hashes are obtained.

- **Password Spraying:** Adversaries may use a single or small list of commonly used passwords against many different accounts to attempt to acquire valid account credentials.

- **Credential Stuffing:** Adversaries may use credentials obtained from breach dumps of unrelated accounts to gain access to target accounts through credential overlap.

In order to answer the question we will need to see what username and password combinations are being used.

We can see the exploit attempts by opening the ``pcap`` in Wireshark and filtering for ``http`` traffic

  **![](data:image/png;base64,)**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**  

As we want to see http conversations we can look at the TCP tab
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

We can see that most of the conversations originate from ``138.199.59.221`` and we are directed towards ``172.31.6.44`` on port ``8080``. 

Since this traffic is not encrypted using HTTPS, we are able to inspect the packet details.
By selecting different samples of these conversations and choosing “Follow Stream”, We can observe the credentials being attempted by the attacker in each request. 

  
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
  **![](data:image/png;base64,)**
  
We can also see the username and password used in the attack in the Wireshark packet details pane. Using the details highlighted in the red rectangle boxes in the screenshot above, we can apply a Wireshark display filter to show only the exploit attempts.

``http.request.uri == "/bonita/loginservice" && http.user_agent =="python-requests/2.28.1"``

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

While manual inspection of individual packets in Wireshark is possible to extract credentials, this method is inefficient for analysing large packet captures (PCAPs). To automate this process and comprehensively identify all authentication attempts, we utilized ``thsark`` the powerful command-line counterpart to Wireshark.

We will use the command below to see each username and password combination used:

``tshark -Y '(http.request.uri == "/bonita/loginservice") && (http.user_agent == "python-requests/2.28.1")' -r meerkat.pcap -T json | jq '.[]._source.layers.http."http.file_data"' | sort | uniq``


**Breakdown of the Command Logic:** 

- **``tshark`` Extraction:**
	- ``-Y '(http.request.uri == "/bonita/loginservice") && (http.user_agent == "python-requests/2.28.1")'`` This display filter precisely targets HTTP POST request containing login credentials sent to the ``/bonita/loginservice`` endpoint by the attackers Python script, effectively filtering out all other network noise.
	- ``-r meerkat.pcap``: specifies the input packet capture file.
	- ``-T jsonn``: Outputs the results in JSON format for structured parsing.
	  
-  **``jq`` Parsing**
	- ``jq '.[]._source.layers.http."http.file_data"'``: This filter drills down into the JSON structure to extract the content of the ``http.file_data`` field, which contains the raw POST data payload, in this case, the JSON formatted username and password.
    
- **Data refinement:**
	- ``| sort | uniq``: The extracted payloads are piped into ``sort`` and then ``uniq``. This is a classic data processing technique to deduplicate the results, presenting a clean, unique list of credential pairs attempted by the attacker.
	  
This methodology demonstrates an efficient, repeatable, and scriptable approach to forensic evidence extraction, transforming a large PCAP file into a concise list of critical indicators (credential pairs) with high precision.

  
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
  

Following the extraction of unique credential pairs, an analysis of the attacker’s methodology was conducted. By classifying the attack pattern, we can better understand the threat actor’s capabilities and intentions. The evidence was evaluated against common brute-force attack definitions:

- **Ruled Out: Password Guessing**
    - **Rationale:** The attack did not use obvious, sequentially guessed credentials (e.g., ``admin:admin``, ``admin:password1``). The extracted list showed varied and non-sequential usernames and password, which is inconsistent with guessing approach

- **Ruled Out: Password Cracking**
	- **Rationale:** The attack was conducted against the application’s login service itself. There was no evidence of intercepted password hashes being exported for offline analysis or cracking attempts.
	  
- **Ruled Out: Password Spraying**
    - **Rationale:** The attacker did not use a single common password across a large list of usernames. Instead, each username was paired with a unique, specific password.
    
**Conclusion: Credential Stuffing Attack**

The evidence strongly indicates a Credential Stuffing Attack. The attacker used a list of username and password pairs that appeared to be valid, real-world credentials (e.g., ``alice:RedRock1``, ``bob:SecurePass2023!``). These pairs, often sourced from previous breaches and sold on the dark web, were systematically tested against the bonita application to exploit the common user behavior of password reuse across multiple services. This classification is consistent with the use of automated tools (as indicated by the Python User-Agent) to test large volumes of pre-complied credential pairs.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

# Which string was appended to the API URL path to bypass the authorization filter by the attacker's exploit?

The vulnerability is explained [here:](https://rhinosecuritylabs.com/application-security/cve-2022-25237-bonitasoft-authorization-bypass/)

This shows the string to be ``i18ntranslation``.

We can also see this in the packet capture by following the http stream of one of the

exploit attempts in the same way we did earlier.

Here we can see the API endpoint to be ``/bonita/API/pageUpload`` and this is appended with ``;i18ntranslation`` This shows the string to be ``i18ntranslation``

We can also see this in the packet capture by following the HTTP stream of one of the exploit attempts in the same way we did earlier. 

here we can see the API endpoint to be ``/bonita/API/pageUpload`` and this is appended

with ``i18ntranslation``

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
  
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
# How many combinations of usernames and passwords were used in the credential stuffing attack?

We can reuse ``tshark`` command and pipe the output to ``wc -l`` to count the lines.

``tshark -Y '(http.request.uri == "/bonita/loginservice") && (http.user_agent == "python-requests/2.28.1")' -r meerkat.pcap -T json | jq '.[]._source.layers.http."http.file_data"' | sort | uniq | wc -l``

Now we have 57 unique combinations of usernames and passwords.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

But this is not the correct answer.

That is why [the exploit](https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/CVEs/blob/master/CVE-2022-25237/CVE-2022-25237.py) always tries the default credentials ``install:install`` every time it runs.
We can see evidence of this in the packet capture.
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

therefore ``install:install`` should be excluded from the credential-stuffing count, so subtract 1 from the unique credentials total.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

# Which username and password combination was successful?
Back in Wireshark, we can see the total packets sent.

We notice that **the average is 18, but a few conversations contain 55 and 58 packets.**

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

We also see ``HTTP`` status code ``204``. 

HTTP status code 204 means “No content”, indicating that the server successfully processed the request but returned no content in the response. 

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

This means that the username ``[seb.broom@forela.co.uk](mailto:seb.broom@forela.co.uk)`` and password ``g0vernm3nt`` were sent successfully, but the server did not return any content.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

# Please provide the filename of the public key used by the attacker to gain persistence on our host.

To resolve the issue, we can browse the [attacker’s pastes](https://pastes.io/raw/bx5gcr0et8) on  [pastes.io](http://pastes.io) 
*(If you browse those pages, be careful — pastes can contain malicious links or scripts.)*

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

When we browse the paste [hffgr4unv](https://pastes.io/raw/hffgra4unv) on pastes.io , we can see the RSA key.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

In circumstances where we want to investigate an artifact that was hosted on the public internet, but is no longer available, we can use [The Wayback Machine](http://web.archive.org/). 
This is useful to know in a real investigation where an attacker has removed their payloads

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
# Can you confirm the file modified by the attacker to gain persistence?

As we saw in the previous section, the attacker gained persistence via an SSH public key. Adding this key to the ``~/.ssh/authorized_keys`` file will allow them to log in to the server via SSH.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
**![](data:image/png;base64,)**

# Can you confirm the MITRE technique ID of this type of persistence mechanism?

Consulting the  [MITRE ATT&CK®](https://attack.mitre.org/) for the persistence tactic we can see the technique ``Account Manipulation`` Which has the sub-technique of ``SSH Authorised Keys``
